examples.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-7t} f(t)\}.$ Show the steps to compute this transform.
examples.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-7t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-7t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+7)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\displaystyle F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+7)t} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t = F(s+7),
$$

where 

$$
s + 7 > s_0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 
s > s_0 - 7.
$$

feedback.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{8t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{8t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $8$ units to the right.

submitted_fields.submitted_value: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $8$ units to the right.
